segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees gathered around him, together with some of the scribes who had come from Jerusalem,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and they saw that some of his disciples were eating bread with defiled hands, that is, unwashed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Pharisees, and all the Jews, do not eat unless they wash their hands with a fistful of water, holding to the tradition of the elders;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and when they come from the marketplace they do not eat unless they immerse themselves. And there are many other things they have received to hold to: immersions of cups and pitchers and bronze vessels and dining couches.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Pharisees and the scribes asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do your disciples not walk according to the tradition of the elders, but eat bread with defiled hands?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Isaiah prophesied well about you hypocrites, as it is written: ‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away from me;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: in vain do they worship me, teaching human commands as doctrines.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Abandoning the commandment of God, you hold to human tradition.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “How well you set aside the commandment of God in order to keep your tradition!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For Moses said, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must be put to death.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you say that if a person tells his father or mother, ‘Whatever support you might have had from me is Corban’—that is, a gift—

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: then you no longer let him do anything for his father or mother,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: nullifying the word of God by your tradition, which you have handed down. And you do many other things of the same kind.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Calling the crowd to him again, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen to me, all of you, and understand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There is nothing outside a person that can defile him by going into him; rather, it is the things that come out of a person that defile a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he had left the crowd and gone into a house, his disciples asked him about the parable.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Are you also so without understanding? Do you not see that nothing going into a person from outside can defile him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: because it does not go into his heart but into his stomach, and goes out into the latrine?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Thus he declared all foods clean.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What comes out of a person, that is what defiles a person.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For from within, out of people’s hearts, come evil thoughts: acts of sexual immorality, thefts, murders,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: adulteries, acts of greed, acts of wickedness, deceit, debauchery, an envious eye, slander, arrogance, folly.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: All these wicked things come from within and defile a person.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: From there he set out and went away to the region of Tyre. He entered a house and did not want anyone to know, but he could not escape notice.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Instead, a woman whose little daughter had an unclean spirit heard about him at once, and she came and fell at his feet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The woman was a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth, and she kept asking him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let the children eat their fill first, for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the little dogs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But she answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Sir, even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because of that answer, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went off to her home and found the child lying on the bed and the demon gone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he left the region of Tyre again and went by way of Sidon to the Sea of Galilee, through the middle of the region of the Decapolis.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They brought him a man who was deaf and could hardly speak, and they begged him to lay his hand on him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Taking him aside privately, away from the crowd, he put his fingers into the man’s ears, and after spitting he touched his tongue.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he looked up to heaven, sighed, and said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Ephphatha,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: which means “Be opened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And his ears were opened, the bond on his tongue was loosed, and he began to speak plainly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He ordered them to tell no one; but the more he ordered them, the more abundantly they proclaimed it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were astonished beyond all measure, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He has done everything well; he makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak.”

notes.note: The Greek word ordinarily means "common" or "shared". In Jewish Greek it had come to mean ritually profane, the opposite of holy or pure, as in 1 Maccabees. Mark explains it for readers unfamiliar with this usage. The issue is ritual purity, not hygiene.

notes.traditional: thoroughly / properly (KJV "oft", from a variant reading)
notes.note: The Greek says literally "with a fist", and what this meant is uncertain. Proposals include washing with a handful of water, with the hand cupped, or up to the wrist; many translations paraphrase as "thoroughly" or "properly". Some manuscripts read "often" instead, probably a copyist's attempt to resolve the difficulty.

This is the verb elsewhere rendered "baptize"; in ordinary Greek it means to dip or plunge, and Jewish writers used it for ritual washing. Most translations say "wash" here, and the verb does not always specify full immersion (compare Luke 11:38). "Immerse" keeps it distinct from the hand-washing verb in verse 3 and suits the vessels that follow. Some early manuscripts read "sprinkle" instead.

notes.traditional: and tables (KJV); omitted or footnoted in many modern versions
notes.note: Several important early manuscripts lack these words, and editors are divided on whether they are original; the SBLGNT includes them. The noun means a bed or a couch for reclining at meals.

Corban is a Hebrew and Aramaic term for an offering dedicated to God, which Mark translates for his readers as "gift". Declaring property Corban worked as a vow that put it off-limits to another person, here one's parents, without it necessarily being handed over to the temple. The details of the practice in Jesus's day are reconstructed partly from later rabbinic sources.

notes.traditional: followed by verse 16: "If any man have ears to hear, let him hear"
notes.note: Verse 16 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is not in the SBLGNT text, so the numbering passes from 15 to 17. It was probably added by copyists on the model of Mark 4:9 and 4:23.

notes.phrase: Thus he declared all foods clean.
notes.traditional: (Thus he declared all foods clean.) / KJV "purging all meats"
notes.note: The Greek is a bare participial phrase, "cleansing all foods". Most scholars and modern translations take it as Mark's own comment with Jesus as its subject, as here. Later manuscripts have a different grammatical form that makes it part of Jesus's sentence, describing digestion or the latrine as "purging" food; the King James Version follows that reading.

notes.traditional: an evil eye (KJV); envy (most modern versions)
notes.note: The Greek says literally "an evil eye", a Semitic idiom for a grudging, envious or stingy disposition. It does not refer to a curse cast by a look, which is what the phrase suggests in modern English. The rendering keeps the image of the eye while giving the sense.

"Greek" here denotes a non-Jew of Greek language and culture, not someone from Greece; many translations say "Gentile". Her origin is given separately as Syrophoenician, that is, from Phoenicia in the Roman province of Syria.

The Greek word is a diminutive, and the woman's reply pictures dogs under the table, so household dogs rather than street scavengers are in view. Whether the diminutive softens the saying is disputed: such forms had often lost their force in Koine, and Mark uses several in this passage. Most interpreters take the children to stand for Israel and the dogs for Gentiles.

The word of address was the ordinary polite "sir" and also the title "Lord". On the lips of a Gentile stranger "Sir" is the natural sense, though Mark's readers may well have heard more in it. This is the only place in Mark where Jesus is addressed this way.

candidates.reason: With its adjective κοινός it recurs in Matthew, Acts, Romans and Hebrews, where translators vary between defile, make unclean, profane and common, obscuring the link between passages.
The word covers stories, short sayings, riddles and comparisons across the Gospels and Hebrews, and "parable" suggests only a story to modern readers.
It recurs in the Gospels, Acts, Paul and Revelation with renderings ranging from fornication to sexual immorality to prostitution, and consistency matters for the divorce and vice-list texts.
It means abusive speech against people in some places and against God in others, and one decision is needed on when to use slander and when blasphemy.
"Scribe" suggests a copyist to modern readers, whereas the word denotes a trained expert in the Jewish law; it is frequent across the Gospels and Acts.
